name: Stiff Person Syndrome

criteria.description: Stiffness in axial muscles (trunk, paraspinal) with prominent lumbar hyperlordosis
Superimposed episodic spasms triggered by sensory stimuli, emotional stress, or startle
Positive anti-GAD65 antibodies (high titers, typically >2,000 IU/mL)
Continuous motor unit activity on EMG in affected muscles that resolves with diazepam
Absence of alternative explanation (structural, neurodegenerative, psychogenic)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Axial stiffness with episodic spasms plus high-titer anti-GAD65 antibodies or positive anti-amphiphysin antibodies. EMG confirmation supportive.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Spectrum includes classic SPS, stiff limb syndrome (focal variant), progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM). Anti-amphiphysin antibodies are paraneoplastic (breast cancer). Anti-glycine receptor antibodies associated with PERM.

pathognomonic.notes: Board-like rigidity of paraspinal muscles; exaggerated lumbar lordosis
Triggered by sudden noise, touch, or emotional stress; can cause falls
Hyperekplexia; whole-body stiffening in response to unexpected stimuli

common.notes: Stiff, slow gait; difficulty turning; robot-like walking
Agoraphobia-like symptoms; fear of falling; anticipatory anxiety worsens spasms
Falls 'like a statue' without protective reflexes

occasional.notes: Tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis during severe spasms
Type 1 diabetes mellitus (~30-40% of GAD-positive SPS patients)

rare.notes: More common in PERM variant (progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus)

laboratory: Anti-GAD65 antibodies at high titers (typically >2,000 IU/mL; often >10,000)
Anti-amphiphysin antibodies (paraneoplastic; associated with breast cancer)
Anti-DPPX antibodies (SPS variant with GI symptoms)
Elevated GAD antibodies in CSF (intrathecal synthesis)
Screen for associated autoimmunity: type 1 diabetes, thyroid disease, pernicious anemia
imaging: Brain and spine MRI typically normal in classic SPS
MRI may show signal changes in PERM variant
other: EMG showing continuous motor unit activity in paraspinal and abdominal muscles at rest
EMG activity resolves or improves with IV diazepam
No voluntary suppression possible of continuous motor activity
Paraneoplastic panel if amphiphysin or atypical presentation

distinguishingFeatures: MS spasticity follows anatomical UMN distribution
MS has demyelinating lesions on MRI
MS does not have continuous motor unit activity on EMG
FND has inconsistent and incongruent findings
FND does not have elevated GAD antibodies
FND does not show continuous EMG activity
SPS is commonly misdiagnosed as FND
HSP has progressive pure spasticity without spasms
HSP does not have anti-GAD or anti-amphiphysin antibodies

redFlags: Anti-amphiphysin antibodies require aggressive cancer screening (especially breast cancer)
Status spasticus (continuous severe spasms) is a medical emergency requiring ICU care
SPS is commonly misdiagnosed as anxiety, conversion disorder, or fibromyalgia - average diagnostic delay is years
Concurrent type 1 diabetes should prompt GAD antibody testing at high titers
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM) variant has brainstem involvement and worse prognosis
Glycine receptor antibodies suggest PERM and require different treatment approach
references: Dalakas MC. Stiff-person syndrome and GAD antibody-spectrum disorders: GABAergic neuronal excitability, immunopathogenesis and update on antibody therapies. Neurotherapeutics. 2022;19(3):832-847.
Baizabal-Carvallo JF, Jankovic J. Stiff-person syndrome: insights into a complex autoimmune disorder. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry. 2015;86(8):840-848.
McKeon A, et al. Stiff-man syndrome and variants. Arch Neurol. 2012;69(2):230-238.
